\mxunit{enrichment-lattice-paths-solutions}{Paths, combinations and Pascal}
\mxsubtitle{High school · counting \textperiodcentered{} Worked solutions \textperiodcentered{} 05}

\begin{exercise}
Find $\binom{8}{2}$ and explain why it equals $\binom{8}{6}$.
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
$\binom{8}{2} = 8 \times  \frac{7}{2} = 28$. Choosing two excluded objects is equivalent to choosing six included objects.
\end{solution}

\begin{exercise}
Count monotone paths from $\pt{0;0}$ to $\pt{4;3}$.
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
Choose four rightward steps among seven: $\binom{7}{4} = 35$.
\end{solution}

\begin{exercise}
How many of these paths pass through $\pt{2;1}$?
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
$\binom{3}{2} \times  \binom{4}{2} = 3 \times  6 = 18$.
\end{solution}

\begin{exercise}
Choose a team of three from eight people. Two specified people cannot be together. How many teams remain possible?
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
There are $\binom{8}{3} = 56$ teams. Exactly 6 contain both specified people. Therefore 50 teams remain.
\end{solution}

\begin{problem}[Investigate, justify, conclude]
Count monotone paths from $\pt{0;0}$ to $\pt{5;4}$ that avoid $A\pt{2;1}$ and $B\pt{3;3}$. Count all paths, then those passing through A, through B and through both. Explain why the last category must be added back.
\end{problem}
\begin{solution}
Total: $\binom{9}{5} = 126$. Through A: $\binom{3}{2}\binom{6}{3} = 60$. Through B: $\binom{6}{3}\binom{3}{2} = 60$. Through both: $3 \times  \binom{3}{1} \times  3 = 27$. Paths through both were subtracted twice; adding them back once gives $126 - 60 - 60 + 27 = 33$.
\end{solution}
